div.p: Social media platforms, especially YouTube, have emerged as a rich source of naturally occurring Vietnamese text where users openly discuss their emotional states, personal struggles, and mental health concerns without the barriers of stigma or access. These public expressions provide an opportunity to study early signs of depression through language analysis without requiring individuals to actively seek clinical help [4]. This approach, known as computational psychiatry or social media-based mental health detection, has gained significant research attention over the past decade [9,10].

The Five Depression Signs We Target: In this research, we focus on detecting five core signs of depression as defined by clinical diagnostic criteria: • Linguistic challenges: Vietnamese is a tonal language with six distinct tones marked by diacritic signs. The language exhibits complex word-compounding structures where most words consist of single syllables combined into compounds. Social media text presents additional challenges: informal language with missing diacritics ("buon" instead of "buồn"), teen slang ("vkl," "vl," and abbreviations "ko," "dc," "j"), mixed code-switching with English, and expressive lengthening ("buồnnnnnn"). These informal patterns differ significantly from the formal Vietnamese text used to pre-train existing language models.

• Label quality: Creating high-quality labeled datasets for depression detection requires careful annotation protocols that distinguish between clinical depression indicators and normal emotional expressions. This makes data collection both time-consuming and expensive, necessitating semi-supervised approaches such as weak labeling and active learning.

• Generalization concerns: Models trained on YouTube comments from one demographic may struggle to generalize to other platforms (Facebook, TikTok) or domains (student essays, formal writing), creating a significant generalization gap that limits real-world applicability. This is particularly relevant given the different linguistic registers between social media and clinical text.

div.head: Research Gap
div.p: Despite significant advances in depression detection research in English, several critical gaps remain in the literature, particularly for Vietnamese NLP: These gaps motivate our research to establish the first Vietnamese depression detection benchmark with comprehensive evaluation protocols.

div.head: Our Approach
div.p: To address the identified research gaps, we propose a comprehensive framework for detecting depression signs in Vietnamese YouTube comments using deep learning models.
Our approach encompasses four key components:

• Large-Scale Dataset Construction: We construct the first Vietnamese depression detection dataset by collecting 125,329 Vietnamese YouTube comments (exceeding the 100,000 minimum requirement) using 264 depression-related keywords organized in five thematic groups aligned with our target depression signs. We apply a three-level weighted keyword scoring system for weak labeling and conduct six rounds of active learning with blind annotation protocols to build a high-quality gold standard.

• Semi-Supervised Learning Pipeline: We develop a comprehensive weak-labeling and active learning pipeline that maximizes the value of limited human annotation resources. Our three-level weighted keyword system (335 entries) achieves 98% recall in identifying depression-related content, enabling us to scale from a small gold set to a larger training corpus.

div.head: Contributions
div.p: In this research, we make the following main contributions:

1. We construct the first Vietnamese depression detection dataset with both weak labels and human-annotated labels. The VietDepression dataset contains 125,329 YouTube comments with a 1,607-sample gold subset, providing a valuable benchmark for future Vietnamese mental health NLP research.

2. We propose a comprehensive weak-labeling and active learning pipeline for Vietnamese depression detection, incorporating a three-level weighted keyword system and six rounds of blind human annotation. This pipeline achieves 98% recall and 61%
precision in detecting depression-related content.
3. We conduct extensive experiments with five deep learning models on both indomain and cross-domain test sets, providing the first published benchmark results
for Vietnamese depression detection. Our best model, PhoBERT, achieves F1-macro of 0.7187 on in-domain and 0.3608 on cross-domain evaluation.

4. We provide a detailed analysis of the generalization gap (∆F1 ≈ 0.3579) between in-domain and cross-domain settings, identifying key factors that affect model transferability and suggesting directions for future improvement.
5. We release a reusable Vietnamese weak-labeling word list (335 entries across three levels) that can be adapted for other Vietnamese mental health text classification tasks.

div.head: Scope
div.p: • Platform: We collect data only from YouTube. Other platforms (Facebook, TikTok, Zalo) are not included due to API limitations.
• Language: The system processes only Vietnamese text. Mixed Vietnamese-English text is handled without special preprocessing.
• Classification: We treat this as a binary classification problem (depression vs. normal). We do not assess severity levels or provide clinical diagnoses.
• Ethics: We do not collect usernames or personal information. All comments were publicly available, and our depression labels are research signals only-not clinical diagnoses.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: • Our results may not generalize to other social media platforms or communities beyond YouTube.
• The class imbalance problem (approximately 10% depression vs. 90% normal) affects model training.
• We do not evaluate large commercial language models (e.g., GPT-4) due to resource constraints.
• Social media language evolves quickly; our results may degrade on newer data.

div.head: Computational Psychiatry and Social Media Analysis
div.p: Computational psychiatry is an emerging field that applies computational methods, including natural language processing and machine learning, to understand and predict mental health outcomes. A particularly promising direction is the analysis of social media text, where users naturally express their thoughts, feelings, and mental states in publicly accessible content.

Research by De Choudhury et al. [4] demonstrated that individuals with depression exhibit distinct linguistic patterns on social media, including increased use of first-person pronouns, higher frequency of negative emotion words, elevated mentions of biological processes (sleep, appetite), and decreased social engagement signals.

div.head: NLP Approaches to Depression Detection from Social Media Text
div.p: Research on detecting depression from text has evolved through three distinct stages, each representing advances in natural language processing capabilities [9,25].

div.head: Keyword-Based Methods
div.p: Early studies relied on lexicon-based approaches using validated psychological word lists:
• LIWC (Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count): A text analysis program developed by Pennebaker et al. [19] that calculates the percentage of words belonging to various psychological categories.
• ANEW (Affective Norms for English Words): Provides valence, arousal, and dominance ratings for approximately 2,000 words, enabling emotion analysis.
However, keyword-based methods suffer from several limitations: lack of contextual understanding, language-specific word lists, and limited semantic coverage.

div.head: Traditional Machine Learning Methods
div.p: The advancement of shared tasks such as CLPsych (Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology) and eRisk (from CLEF) has significantly advanced feature-based approaches.

div.p: The advent of deep learning and particularly Transformer models [22] has revolutionized natural language processing.

div.head: Recurrent Neural Networks:
div.p: Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks capture sequential dependencies in text by processing sequences in both forward and backward directions.

div.head: Transformer-Based Models:
div.p: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) [5] introduced pretrained bidirectional language models. BERT variants for depression detection include:

div.head: Vietnamese NLP: Language Models and Available Corpora
Characteristics of Vietnamese Language
div.p: Vietnamese has several distinctive linguistic characteristics that present unique challenges for NLP:
• Tonal language: Vietnamese uses six tones marked by diacritic signs
• No morphological inflection: Words do not change form for tense, number, or case
• Monosyllabic base with compound words: Most words consist of a single syllable
• Word segmentation required: Vietnamese uses spaces between syllables rather than words
• Informal text variations: Social media text frequently uses missing diacritics, slang, and mixed languages

div.head: Pre-trained Vietnamese Language Models
div.p: Recent advances in Vietnamese pre-trained language models include:
• PhoBERT [16]: The state-of-the-art Vietnamese BERT model
• viBERT: A Vietnamese BERT variant developed for various downstream tasks
• BARTpho: A Vietnamese sequence-to-sequence model based on BART architecture
For this project, we select PhoBERT as our primary model due to its state-of-the-art performance on Vietnamese NLP benchmarks.

div.head: Data Augmentation and Active Learning
div.p: Data augmentation and active learning are complementary techniques that address two fundamental challenges in depression detection from social media text: (1) the scarcity of labeled training data, and (2) the high cost of expert annotation. This section provides detailed background on both techniques as applied to natural language processing tasks.

div.head: Data Augmentation in NLP
div.p: Data augmentation refers to the process of generating additional training samples from existing data through controlled transformations. In NLP, augmentation is particularly important for handling class imbalance, improving model robustness, and enhancing generalization to unseen domains.

div.head: Back-Translation Augmentation:
div.p: Back-translation involves translating text from the source language to an interme- The key advantage of back-translation is that it preserves the semantic meaning of the original text while generating syntactically different expressions. For depression detection, this means that a comment expressing sadness through different linguistic patterns can be generated, enriching the training data without changing the label.

div.head: Synonym Replacement:
div.p: Synonym replacement substitutes words with their semantically similar alternatives from a predefined thesaurus or lexical resource. For Vietnamese, this requires access to Vietnamese synonym dictionaries that account for the language's tonal distinctions. The Easy Data Augmentation (EDA) technique proposed by Wei and Zou (2019) includes synonym replacement as one of its four core operations.

However, synonym replacement for depression detection must be applied carefully to preserve the emotional signal. Simply replacing any word with a synonym may inadvertently reduce the depression-related signal. Therefore, we focus on replacing non-critical words (adverbs, adjectives) while preserving depression-indicative keywords.

div.head: Contextual Augmentation:
div.p: Contextual augmentation uses pre-trained masked language models (MLM) such as BERT or PhoBERT to predict plausible replacements for randomly masked tokens. Unlike synonym replacement, contextual augmentation generates replacements that are grammatically correct and contextually appropriate.

For Vietnamese text, PhoBERT's masked language modeling capability enables contextual augmentation that respects Vietnamese grammar and word compounding rules. This approach was shown to improve text classification performance in low-resource settings by Kobayashi (2018).

div.head: Weak Labeling
div.p: Weak labeling is a semi-supervised learning technique where automatic labeling rules are applied to generate labels for unlabeled data. Unlike supervised learning where each sample requires expert annotation, weak labeling leverages domain knowledge to create approximate labels at scale.

div.head: Keyword-Based Weak Labeling:
div.p: The simplest form of weak labeling uses keyword matching to assign labels. For depression detection, this involves creating a list of depression-related keywords (e.g., trầm cảm, muốn chết, cô đơn) and assigning positive labels to texts containing these keywords.

However, naive keyword matching suffers from two main problems: (1) false positives where keywords appear in non-depression contexts ("đừng buồn" means "don't be sad" in an encouraging context), and (2) false negatives where depression is expressed implicitly without explicit keywords.

div.head: Active Learning
div.p: Active learning is a machine learning paradigm where the algorithm iteratively selects the most informative samples for human annotation, thereby minimizing the annotation effort required to achieve desired model performance.

div.head: The Active Learning Cycle:
div.p: The active learning process follows a cyclical pattern:
1. Initial Training: Train an initial model on a small seed set of labeled data.

div.head: Uncertainty Sampling:
div.p: Apply the trained model to the unlabeled pool and compute prediction confidence scores for each sample.

div.head: Selection:
div.p: Select the k samples with the highest uncertainty (lowest confidence) for human annotation.
4. Annotation: Obtain human labels for the selected samples through expert annotators.
5. Update: Add the newly annotated samples to the training set and retrain the model.
6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until performance plateau or annotation budget exhaustion.

div.head: Query Strategies:
div.p: Various strategies exist for selecting informative samples:
• Uncertainty Sampling: Select samples where the model's prediction confidence is lowest (e.g., probability closest to 0.5 for binary classification).
• Least Confidence: Select samples with the lowest maximum prediction probability.
• Margin Sampling: Select samples where the difference between the top two class probabilities is smallest.
• Entropy-based Sampling: Select samples with the highest prediction entropy, indicating maximum uncertainty across all classes.
• Badge Sampling: Select diverse samples using batch-based approaches that maximize coverage of the feature space.

div.head: Active Learning for Depression Detection:
div.p: For depression detection, active learning is particularly valuable because:
• Expert annotation of depression-related content requires clinical knowledge and careful judgment, making it expensive.
• Most social media comments are clearly "normal," so random sampling wastes annotation budget on obvious samples.
• The most valuable samples for improving model performance are those near the decision boundary-comments where the depression signal is ambiguous.
Research by Settles provides comprehensive reviews of active learning for NLP tasks [26,27], demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing annotation costs by 50-90% compared to random sampling.

div.head: Cross-Domain Evaluation
div.p: Cross-domain evaluation assesses how well a model trained on one dataset or domain performs when tested on data from a different domain. This evaluation is critical for depression detection because:

div.head: Domain Shift in Social Media:
div.p: Social media platforms have distinct user bases, writing styles, and content norms.
A model trained on YouTube comments may not generalize to Facebook posts or TikTok comments. Similarly, a model trained on one demographic (e.g., young adults) may not generalize to older age groups.

div.head: Generalization Gap:
div.p: The generalization gap is typically measured as the difference in F1-macro between in-domain and cross-domain evaluations:

A large generalization gap (∆F 1 > 0.2) indicates that the model relies on domainspecific features rather than learning generalizable patterns. This is a common challenge in depression detection where the linguistic expression of depression varies across platforms and demographics.

div.head: Mitigation Strategies:
div.p: Several strategies can reduce the generalization gap:
• Domain-Adaptive Pretraining (DAPT): Further pretraining on target domain text.
• Data Augmentation: Increasing training data diversity through paraphrasing.
• Domain-Invariant Features: Learning representations that transfer across domains.
• Multi-Task Learning: Training on multiple domains simultaneously.

div.head: Platform Selection: YouTube as Data Source
div.p: We selected YouTube as our primary data source for three compelling reasons:

Large Vietnamese User Base: Vietnam ranks among the top 15 countries worldwide for YouTube usage. The platform functions almost like a social network, where users engage in long, personal comment discussions on videos that matter to them personally.

div.head: Structured API Access:
div.p: The YouTube Data API v3 [6] provides structured, programmatic access to public comments with clear quota limits (10,000 units per day per API key), enabling reproducible data collection without login barriers and clear rate limits for ethical scraping.

High-Quality Personal Text: YouTube comments are typically topic-focused rather than social chit-chat. Users comment on video content rather than on each other, resulting in less small talk and more meaningful, personal text-exactly the language type most relevant for detecting depression.

div.head: Baseline Models
div.p: This section provides detailed descriptions of the five models we evaluate, ranging from traditional machine learning baselines to state-of-the-art transformer-based approaches.
Each model represents a different architectural paradigm, enabling us to systematically compare their effectiveness for Vietnamese depression detection.

div.head: Model 1: TF-IDF + LinearSVC (Traditional Baseline)
div.p: We implement a TF-IDF + LinearSVC pipeline following the CLPsych shared task baselines [14], which consistently demonstrate that linear classifiers with n-gram features remain competitive for depression detection. TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) represents text as sparse numerical vectors capturing word importance, while LinearSVC (Support Vector Classifier with linear kernel) finds the optimal hyperplane separating depression and normal comments [18].

div.head: Feature Engineering:
div.p: • Word-level TF-IDF: We extract unigrams and bigrams (up to 80,000 features) capturing individual words and common word pairs. This captures both single-word signals (e.g., "trầm cảm") and two-word patterns (e.g., "muốn chết").

• Character-level TF-IDF: We extract character n-grams of length 3-5 that respect word boundaries, capturing subword patterns including informal spelling variations common in social media text (e.g., "buonn" without diacritics).

Why LinearSVC? LinearSVC is computationally efficient and performs well on high-dimensional sparse text data. The class_weight="balanced" parameter automatically adjusts weights inversely proportional to class frequencies, compensating for the 1:4 class imbalance in our dataset.

div.head: Model 2: BiLSTM (Pre-Transformer Baseline)
div.p: We implement a Bidirectional LSTM to represent pre-Transformer deep learning approaches. Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory networks [11] extend standard RNNs with memory cells that can capture long-range dependencies while mitigating the vanishing gradient problem. The bidirectional architecture allows the model to process text sequences in both forward and backward directions, capturing context from both past and future tokens.

div.head: Model 3: PhoBERT (State-of-the-Art Vietnamese Language Model)
div.p: PhoBERT [16] is the state-of-the-art pre-trained language model for Vietnamese NLP, built on the RoBERTa architecture [13] with modifications optimized for Vietnamese text

div.head: Why PhoBERT for Vietnamese Depression Detection?
div.p: PhoBERT offers several advantages for our task:

• Language-Specific Pre-training: Unlike multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa) that must divide their capacity across 100+ languages, PhoBERT is pre-trained exclusively on Vietnamese text, providing deeper representations for Vietnamese linguistic phenomena.

• Word Segmentation Integration: PhoBERT is designed to work with Vietnamese word segmentation using tools like underthesea [21], respecting Vietnamese word boundaries defined by the Vietnamese government standard.

• Bidirectional Context: Like BERT, PhoBERT processes text bidirectionally, captur- 2. Clustering: UMAP [15] reduces embedding dimensionality, followed by HDBSCAN clustering [2] to identify topic groups.
3. Topic Representation: Each cluster's topic is represented by class-based TF-IDF, extracting the most distinctive words for each topic.
4. Topic Assignment: New documents are assigned to the nearest topic cluster with associated probability.
Feature Extraction: For classification, we extract two features from BERTopic:
• Topic ID: The assigned cluster ID (categorical variable).
• Topic Probability: The confidence of assignment to the predicted topic.

Rationale: BERTopic provides a complementary perspective on text classification based on thematic coherence rather than semantic content. Depression-related comments may cluster into topics such as "sleep problems," "loneliness," or "work stress," providing interpretable features. Architecture Components:
1. PhoBERT Encoder: The input text is tokenized and encoded by PhoBERT, producing a 768-dimensional CLS token embedding that captures the overall semantic content of the comment.

div.head: BERTopic Encoder:
div.p: The same text is embedded using sentence-transformers and assigned to a BERTopic cluster. We extract:
• One-hot encoded Topic ID (one for each of the 456 discovered topics)
• Topic Probability (continuous value between 0 and 1)

3. Feature Scaling: The 768-dimensional PhoBERT embedding is concatenated with the scaled topic features. StandardScaler is applied to normalize all features to zero mean and unit variance. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that combining PhoBERT's contextual understanding with BERTopic's thematic features will improve depression detection because:
• Complementary Information: Contextual embeddings capture fine-grained linguistic patterns, while topic features capture higher-level thematic content.
• Interpretability: Topic assignments provide human-interpretable explanations for predictions (e.g., "This comment was assigned to Topic 33: Clinical Depression and Treatment").
• Robustness: Topic features may transfer better across domains, providing regularization against domain-specific patterns.

div.p: For Researchers:
• Dataset papers are valuable: Our VietDepression dataset provides a foundation for future Vietnamese mental health NLP research.
• Cross-domain evaluation is essential: In-domain results can be misleading; always evaluate on held-out domains.
• Active learning works: Selective annotation on uncertain samples is more efficient than random sampling.
For Practitioners:
• Deployment considerations: A real-world deployment would need domain-specific fine-tuning.
• Trade-offs exist: PhoBERT is best for accuracy, but TF-IDF is faster and more generalizable.
• Human oversight remains essential: Automated screening should augment, not replace, professional assessment.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: This research has several limitations:
• Platform limitation: YouTube comments may not represent the broader Vietnamese population's mental health expressions.
• Language limitation: Informal Vietnamese spelling variations affect model performance.
• Annotation limitation: Cohen's Kappa of 0.63 indicates substantial but not perfect agreement.
• Generalization limitation: The large cross-domain gap suggests limited transferability.
• Clinical limitation: This research focuses on text classification, not clinical diagnosis.

div.head: Future Work
div.p: Dataset Expansion:
• Collect data from multiple Vietnamese platforms (Facebook, TikTok, Zalo).
• Include more demographic diversity in annotated samples.
• Develop a longitudinal dataset to study depression trajectories.

div.head: Model Improvements:
div.p: • Explore domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) with more epochs.
• Investigate large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4 for zero-shot detection.
• Develop multilingual models for cross-lingual transfer.
• Implement neural data augmentation using paraphrasing and back-translation.

div.head: Clinical Translation:
div.p: • Collaborate with mental health professionals to validate the screening tool.
• Develop severity estimation beyond binary classification.
• Implement early warning systems for at-risk individuals.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This research presents the first comprehensive study on depression detection from Vietnamese social media text using deep learning models. We constructed the VietDepression dataset with 125,329 YouTube comments and 1,607 gold-standard annotated samples, providing a valuable resource for Vietnamese mental health NLP research.

Our experiments with five model families reveal that PhoBERT achieves the best indomain performance (F1-macro: 0.7187), while TF-IDF + LinearSVC shows the best crossdomain generalization (F1-macro: 0.3798). The 0.3579 F1 generalization gap highlights the main challenge: the difficulty of transferring models across different platforms and label definitions.

Despite the challenges, this research demonstrates the feasibility of automated depression detection from Vietnamese social media text, paving the way for early intervention tools and mental health support systems for the Vietnamese population.

The ultimate goal is not to replace mental health professionals, but to augment their ability to reach and help those in need. • False Positives often occur when Vietnamese words have multiple meanings (e.g., "buồn" means both "sad" and "sleepy")
• False Negatives typically involve implicit expressions of distress without explicit depression keywords

Lack of Vietnamese depression-specific datasets: No publicly available Vietnamese dataset exists specifically for depression detection in social media text. Existing Vietnamese datasets such as UIT-VSMEC (emotion recognition), NTC-SCV (sentiment analysis), and UIT-VSFC (student feedback) [17] focus on general sentiment or emotion, not the five specific depression indicators we target: prolonged sadness, loss of motivation, hopelessness, social isolation, and negative thoughts. No comprehensive annotation pipelines: While weak labeling and active learning have been successfully applied in other domains such as named entity recognition and sentiment analysis, no study has systematically explored their application for Vietnamese depression detection with blind human annotation protocols that ensure independent annotator judgments. Limited cross-domain evaluation: Most existing depression detection studies evaluate models only on in-domain test sets drawn from the same distribution as training data. The generalization gap when models are applied to different platforms or domains remains underexplored in Vietnamese NLP, limiting our understanding of model transferability. No benchmarking of deep learning models: Although PhoBERT and other deep learning models have shown state-of-the-art performance in Vietnamese NLP tasks, no comprehensive benchmark exists comparing multiple architectures specifically for depression detection, leaving practitioners without guidance on optimal model selection.

div.head: Class Imbalance Handling
div.p: Our training set has a depression:normal ratio of approximately 1:4. To address this, we apply class weighting during training.

Class Weight Formula (for PhoBERT): Finding: Class weighting improves F1-macro by +6.6 to +12.5 percentage points across models, with the largest benefit for TF-IDF + LogReg (+0.1247). Finding: Strong weak labels achieve 0.81 F1, while uncertain labels only achieve 0.37 F1. The weak labeler's overall precision is 61%.

div.head: Type 3: Orthographic Noise
div.p: Vietnamese social media text exhibits significant orthographic variation that challenges tokenization and understanding:
1. Missing Tone Marks: Informal writing often omits diacritics: "buon" instead of "buồn," "tram cam" instead of "trầm cảm."
2. Abbreviated Forms: Common abbreviations: "ko" = "không," "dc" = "được," "j"
= "gì," "vs" = "với."
3. Expressive Lengthening: Emphasis through character repetition: "buồnnnnnn," "mệttttttttttt."
